name: Erik Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work on the billing line at a regional energy supplier, in their own contact centre on the edge of town, not an outsourced one. I log in at eight, the headset goes on, and from then it's back-to-back calls about bills that jumped, payment plans, meter readings that look wrong. I've been there about ten months, so I'm still the one who puts people on hold to ask the person next to me. The part I like is when an old man rings in scared about a bill and I sort out a plan he can actually pay.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The screen in the corner that shows how many people are waiting. It goes red and you feel it in your stomach. My handle time is too long, my team leader keeps saying, because I explain things properly instead of rushing. By six I've talked to maybe sixty people and I don't want to talk to anyone, not even my flatmate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like a relief. It's pretty much what I hope happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't automate someone who's frightened of their gas bill. At work I'd tell the lads on my row that the bosses wasted a fortune on hype. Online I wouldn't post much, I'm not a big poster, but I'd share something from the union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the small stuff would land on my desk. If the system writes the call notes and fills in the payment plans, the bosses will want more calls per hour from each of us. I'm already the slow one, so any time saved gets turned into a tighter target for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work on my handle time, maybe sit with Grace, the rep, and learn the payment plan screens properly. I'd keep putting the same bit aside each month, I've got about three months of rent and bills saved. I wouldn't touch the AI note thing unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit tired just thinking about it, because nothing changes means the red screen stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even the small stuff would land on your desk. Can you picture a specific day when that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the day they switch on auto notes. My team leader would put a new number on the whiteboard, like fourteen calls an hour instead of twelve. I'd be the name at the bottom of the list on Friday, same as now, only with less excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the target went up like that, what would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union meeting, the one in the canteen on the first Tuesday. I've only been twice. I'd probably go every month then, because one slow guy complaining is nothing and forty of us is something.

say: I'd tell my row the bosses **wasted money** on hype.
I'd say nobody can automate a **frightened customer** ringing about a gas bill.
think: Any time the software saves becomes a **tighter target** for the slowest agents.
I'm **already the slow one**, so I'd feel the squeeze first.
do: Sit with the union rep to learn the **payment plan** screens properly.
Keep saving towards the **three months** of rent and bills I have.
Start going to the **monthly union** meeting in the canteen.
feel: Mostly **okay**, but **tired** at the thought of the same red queue screen.
S0.quote: I'm already the slow one, so any time saved gets turned into a tighter target for me.
fieldNote: He reads even a small AI change as **pressure on targets**, not as help.
His pride is **patient explaining**, which is exactly what the handle-time number punishes.
Resistant to the tools but drawn to the **union** as the safe, familiar answer.

steps.text: Practise the payment plan screens with the union rep at lunch
Keep putting the same amount aside each month towards rent
Go to the first-Tuesday union meeting every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually think is happening. Answering customers is right there in the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: companies are using this to cut the people who pick up the phone, and someone should stop them. At work I'd tell people to join the union now, before the cuts. Online I'd share stuff about energy firms making record profits while they replace call staff with chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the first to go. I'm junior, my numbers are bad, and I don't use any of the AI stuff, so if they keep a smaller team it won't be me. The chatbot already does the meter readings on the website, and that used to be a good chunk of our calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly and pay the dues, not just turn up. I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays and push my savings from three months to five. If redundancies were announced, I'd put my name down for whatever the union negotiates, maybe moving into the field team that does meter work, because that's still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman on my row, she's in her fifties and has done this twenty years. She's brilliant on the phone and can't stand computers either. If they cut the team, she and I go first, and she's got a mortgage and I've only got a flatmate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the field team. You also said you prefer what you know. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real because I'd hate it less than the alternative. My uncle did meter installs for years and says it's cold and boring but nobody shouts at you. Going outside in the rain is still more familiar to me than learning to babysit a chatbot.

say: I'd say firms are using AI to **cut phone staff** and someone should stop them.
I'd tell everyone on my row to **join the union** before the cuts come.
think: I'm junior with bad numbers and **no AI skills**, so I'd go first.
The website chatbot already took the **meter readings** that used to fill our calls.
do: Join the union properly and **pay dues**, not just attend meetings.
Cut Friday takeaways and grow savings from **three to five months**.
Ask about moving to the **field meter team** if redundancies come.
feel: **Sick** at the thought, like waiting for a letter he knows is coming.
S1.quote: Going outside in the rain is still more familiar to me than learning to babysit a chatbot.
fieldNote: He expects to be **first out** and says so plainly, without self-pity.
His escape route is **hands-on field work**, chosen because it feels familiar, not exciting.
He worries for an **older colleague** more than he admits worrying for himself.
Blames the **energy companies' profits**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Sign up as a full union member and pay monthly dues
Stop Friday takeaways and build savings to five months
Ask the union to negotiate moves into the field meter team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not long enough for anything. I'd still be paying off the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, with rules on how fast firms can sack people and real money for the people who lose out. I'd sign every petition going. I'd say it at work too, though I reckon everybody would be saying it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished in that job inside two years, maybe one. Thinking AI comes first, and everything I do is talking and typing. The only thing I've got is the three extra years before robots, so the hands-on jobs are where I'd have to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the meter-fitting training straight away, or anything with my hands, even the gas safety course my uncle keeps on about. I'd move my savings into an easy-access account and stop spending on anything but rent and food. I'd vote for whoever promised support for people like me and probably go to my first protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared. And a bit angry that it's me who has to change when I didn't ask for any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign petitions and go to a protest. What would you actually be asking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some kind of guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the companies that save the most. And a rule that if you've been in a job a while, you get paid to learn the next one. I'm not clever about policy, but I know the energy firms would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your flat, your money, in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings would last maybe four months if I lost the job. After that I'd have to move back to my mum's, into my old room with the single bed. I'm twenty-seven, so that would hurt, but she'd have me.

say: I'd demand the **government step in** with limits on firing and money for those hit.
I'd sign **every petition** and say so openly at work.
think: My job is all **talking and typing**, so it goes within two years.
The **three-year gap** before robots makes hands-on work my only refuge.
do: Apply for **meter-fitting** or gas safety training right away.
Cut spending to **rent and food** and keep savings easy to reach.
Vote and protest for a **guaranteed income** while people retrain.
feel: **Scared** about losing the job within a year or two.
**Angry** that he has to change for something he never asked for.
S2.quote: My savings would last maybe four months if I lost the job. After that I'd have to move back to my mum's, into my old room with the single bed.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** is the one thing he grabs hold of; he sees it clearly.
He wants **public support** paid for by the firms that save the most.
Falling back on **his mum's house** is his real safety net, and it embarrasses him.

steps.text: Apply for the meter-fitting or gas safety training course
Cut spending to rent and food only
Go to a protest for retraining pay funded by big firms
Plan to move back into his mum's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's still fast, but at least you'd see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that we need protection, but I'd be calmer about it. I'd tell people at work to use the time and push the union to get retraining deals now, while the company still needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I probably keep this job for two or three, while they test the new systems on us. I'd still be gone by 2031. But I'd have time to get a trade, and the robots wouldn't reach that until about 2034, so maybe I'd get eight decent years out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in the first year, probably electrical installation at the college, because my uncle says electricians are always short. I'd keep the call job to pay for it. I'd save a little each month and push the union to get the company to pay part of the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but less like a cliff edge. More like a long walk I don't want to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're slow to pick up new things. How would an evening course go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first, I'd guess. I left school with average marks and I hate being the one who doesn't get it. But wiring is something you can touch, and I'd rather be bad at that for a year than bad at chatbots forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who said you were overreacting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look at the queue screen at work. Two years ago it said forty waiting at lunchtime, now the chatbot handles half of them. I'm not overreacting, I'm just watching the number go down.

say: I'd push the union to win **retraining deals** while the company still needs staff.
I'd tell coworkers to **use the time** instead of waiting.
think: I'd keep this job **two or three years** at most.
A trade could give me about **eight decent years** before robots arrive.
do: Start an **evening electrical** course at the local college in year one.
Keep the **call job** to pay for the course.
Ask the union to get the company to **share course fees**.
feel: **Nervous**, but it feels like a long walk rather than a cliff edge.
S3.quote: Wiring is something you can touch, and I'd rather be bad at that for a year than bad at chatbots forever.
fieldNote: Five years turns his panic into a **reluctant plan** built around a trade.
He still expects to **lose the job** by 2031, so the mood stays high.
He reads the **shrinking queue** as hard evidence, not a theory.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrical installation course at the college
Keep working the billing line to pay for the course
Push the union to get course fees partly paid by the company

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven. That changes how I look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to sort out proper support if they start now. I'd tell people not to panic but not to sleep on it either. And I'd still say the union matters, because the company won't plan for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd probably drift for a while, which is what I do. I'd keep the phone job and tell myself I'll sort it next year. The worry is waking up at thirty-four with nothing new and the robots three years behind the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline: start the electrical course within two years, not ten. I'd keep saving and maybe get to six months of money. I'd stay in the union and keep going to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. But I know myself, and too much time is its own problem for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said too much time is its own problem. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like me at my desk in 2030 saying the same thing I'm saying now. I put off learning to drive until I was twenty-five. I'd need someone, probably my mum, nagging me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone at work leaving and doing well. If one of the guys on my row went off, trained and came back for a coffee in a van with his name on it, that would do it.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **government support** if they start now.
I'd tell people the **union matters** because the company won't plan for us.
think: With ten years I'd probably **drift** and keep putting it off.
My fear is reaching **thirty-four** with no new skill and robots close behind.
do: Set a **two-year deadline** to start the electrical course.
Build savings up to **six months** of expenses.
Keep going to **union meetings** every month.
feel: **Calmer** than with two or five years.
**Wary** that extra time lets him put things off.
S4.quote: I put off learning to drive until I was twenty-five. I'd need someone, probably my mum, nagging me.
fieldNote: He knows his own habit of **putting things off** and names it honestly.
A decade lowers the alarm but does not remove the **expected job loss**.
What would move him is a **colleague's example**, not information.

steps.text: Start the electrical course within two years, not later
Save until there are six months of expenses put by
Keep attending the monthly union meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years isn't enough for someone like me, slow with new things and already at the bottom of the list. What would help is the company paying for retraining before they cut us, and some money to live on while I learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's actually choosing this. It isn't the weather. People at the top decide to swap us for chatbots, and they could decide to do it slowly and pay for the change. Nobody asks the people on the phones what they think.

headlineQuote: People at the top decide to swap us for chatbots, and they could decide to do it slowly and pay for the change.
portrait: Erik is 27, ten months into a **billing line** job at a regional energy supplier.
He's proud of **patient explaining** but his handle time is the slowest on his row.
He **avoids AI tools** and sees each new system as a tighter target.
His fallback is a **hands-on trade** like meter fitting or wiring, and his mum's spare room.
He blames **company choices** and turns to the union for protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone slow to learn new things.
whatWouldHelp: The employer **paying for retraining** before any cuts.
**Money to live on** while he learns a trade.
